outcome: The existence question remains open. Three lines of work appeared in the window: (1) a June 2025 preprint by Frank Vega claims a full proof by contradiction that no quasiperfect number exists, but it is unreviewed, has zero evaluations on Sciety/preprints.org, is on a non-peer-reviewed platform, and its author has a long track record of unaccepted claimed resolutions of famous open problems (P vs NP, generalized forms of the Riemann Hypothesis), so it cannot be treated as resolving anything; (2) a legitimate January 2026 arXiv paper by Max A. Alekseyev raises the numerical lower bound on a hypothetical quasiperfect number from 10^35 to 10^45 via classical computational number theory (SageMath, recursively enumerated sets, MapReduce), no AI involved; (3) an August 2026 arXiv preprint by Toyohara, Tao and Yao raises the minimum number of distinct prime factors from 7 (Hagis-Cohen 1982) to 8, via three elementary lemmas plus a large (79.75-million-leaf) computational elimination verified across CPU/GPU architectures and partially formalized in Lean (259 theorems, zero sorry); an independent 'Pith' desk review recommends peer review and release of computational artifacts before the result is trusted, since the enumeration cannot yet be independently replayed. None of these settles the existence question itself, and I found no credible AI involvement in any of the three: Vega's proof is claimed as human elementary number theory with no tool disclosure, Alekseyev's bound is explicitly classical computer algebra, and the Toyohara/Tao/Yao paper's own text mentions only classical HPC (CPU/GPU enumeration) and a Lean formalization, with no author statement crediting an AI system for producing any of the mathematics. A superficially related GitHub repository (fderuiter/quasiperfect) is built heavily by an AI coding agent ('google-labs-stitch[bot]' via a tool called 'Jitro') but it is a distinct, unconnected project by a different author (Frederick de Ruiter) claiming a different, seemingly unfinished result (a bound with a literal unresolved template placeholder '10^{TelemetryMaxLog}' and a claimed omega(N)>=15 threshold) and must not be conflated with the arXiv paper.

disputes.summary: Frank Vega's June 2025 preprint claims full resolution (non-existence), which if accepted would supersede both later partial-progress papers entirely, but it has received zero independent evaluations and is by an author whose past claimed resolutions of famous problems (P vs NP, Riemann Hypothesis variants) have not been accepted by the mathematical community. I treat it as unverified rather than as the decisive event, and instead date the record to the most credible dated progress (the August 2026 prime-factor bound), while flagging that if Vega's proof were ever validated it would immediately make the whole record 'resolved'.

An unrelated GitHub repository (fderuiter/quasiperfect) tackling the same problem is developed almost entirely through AI-agent-authored pull requests (bot 'google-labs-stitch[bot]', tool 'Jitro'), but its claimed result and authorship do not match the arXiv paper by Toyohara/Tao/Yao; there is no primary-source evidence linking the two projects, despite superficial topical overlap (both use Lean + GPU/CPU search on the same problem). I did not credit the arXiv paper's mathematics to this AI-heavy repository.

summary: Wikipedia's frozen statement asks only whether quasiperfect numbers exist; as of today they are still neither found nor ruled out by anything the mathematical community has vetted. Three results appeared in the window. Frank Vega (preprints.org, June 2025) claims a full proof by contradiction that no quasiperfect number exists; this would resolve the problem outright, but the venue is non-peer-reviewed, the article shows zero evaluations on Sciety, and Vega has a documented history (via ResearchGate, Cambridge Engage, and IPI Letters listings) of claiming resolutions to Millennium-Prize-tier problems that the field has not accepted, so I do not treat this as settling anything and classify it only as an unreviewed claim rather than the basis for 'resolved' or even 'claimed' status for the whole record — I nonetheless log it, since it is the most dramatic thing anyone has said about this problem in the window. Max Alekseyev (arXiv 2601.17832, submitted 2026-01-25) is a legitimate, established computational number theorist whose paper uses a general SageMath-based method to raise the known numerical lower bound on a hypothetical quasiperfect number from 10^35 to 10^45 — a real, if narrow, quantitative bound movement, done with classical computer algebra and no AI. Toyohara, Tao and Yao (arXiv 2608.02066, submitted 2026-08-03) raise the long-standing minimum-prime-factor bound from 7 (1982) to 8, via elementary lemmas plus a large computational elimination (381 'stems' expanding to ~79.75 million 'leaves', verified across seven independently closed computation ledgers on three CPU/GPU architectures) and a partial Lean formalization (259 theorems, zero 'sorry'); an independent desk review on pith.science calls the lemmas sound but flags that the core enumeration cannot yet be independently replayed and recommends peer review plus release of artifacts before full trust — this is 'partial'-grade progress on a case (a stronger necessary condition), not yet expert-digested, so I record the overall status as 'progress' driven by this dated, most-credible advance, while noting Vega's undigested stronger claim in `disputes` rather than letting it drive the record. On AI involvement: I read the arXiv abstract/metadata for both legitimate 2026 papers and found no author statement crediting an AI system with producing any lemma, proof, construction, or bound — the described tools are SageMath, Rust/GPU/CPU enumeration, and Lean, none of which are AI systems under the codes in this task. I could not fetch the full PDF text of either 2026 paper as clean prose (arxiv.org/pdf returns only partially-parseable binary via my fetch tool, and preprints.org/researchgate blocked me with 403s), so my reading of methodology and acknowledgements rests on abstracts, the Pith review's summary, and search-engine syntheses of the abstracts rather than a full read of the PDFs — this is disclosed as a limitation below. I also investigated a coincidentally similar GitHub repository (fderuiter/quasiperfect) that is heavily built by an AI coding agent ('google-labs-stitch[bot]', invoked via a tool named 'Jitro') and initially worried it might be the uncredited engineering substrate behind the Toyohara/Tao/Yao paper; on inspection its claimed result (omega(N)>=15, with an unresolved template artifact '10^{TelemetryMaxLog}' in its own abstract) and its sole author (Frederick de Ruiter) do not match the arXiv paper at all, and no primary source ties the two together, so I did not attribute any AI involvement to the arXiv paper on that basis.
competing_reading: If Vega's June 2025 proof is eventually validated by experts, the correct status becomes 'resolved' (with resolution_direction 'refuted', since the conjecture that they might exist would be answered in the negative) and this entire record should be superseded — the two 2026 papers would become moot, historically-interesting partial results en route to a resolution that had, in fact, already happened five months before either was written. Conversely, if Vega's proof turns out to contain the kind of elementary error that has been found in his other claimed resolutions of famous problems, 'progress' anchored on the August 2026 prime-factor bound is the right call, as I have made it. I lean toward the latter given the base rate of this author's claims, but flag this is a judgment call under uncertainty, not a settled fact — I was not able to obtain a substantive third-party critique of Vega's specific argument (only its absence of peer review), so I cannot rule out that it is correct on the merits.
what_would_settle_it: A named-expert digestion (blog post, MathOverflow thread, or referee report) of Vega's June 2025 argument that either validates or refutes it; alternatively, publication of Vega's paper in (or rejection from) a refereed journal. Separately, for the Toyohara/Tao/Yao result: release and independent replay of the computational artifacts behind the 79.75-million-leaf enumeration, and a completed (not partial) Lean formalization, per the Pith desk review's own recommendation.
